title: The Quiet Collapse of the Centre Ground
standfirst: Both main parties are losing the voters they once took for granted.

readingList.title: The Disappearing Middle: Party Loyalty in Decline
Local Elections Are Telling Us Something

body: For most of the last century, British politics was a contest for the middle. Two large parties, each with a loyal base, fought over a band of floating voters who decided elections. Win them and you won the country. That arrangement is quietly coming apart.

A generation ago, how your parents voted was a fair guide to how you would vote. Class, region and religion did much of the work. Those signals are weaker now. Voters change their minds more often, and they are more willing to lend their vote to a smaller party for one election and take it back at the next.

This matters because both main parties were built on the assumption of a reliable core. Their organisation, their messaging and even their policy offers were designed to hold the base and reach a little beyond it. When the base itself starts to move, that model stops working.
## The middle is not where it was

The other change is subtler. The voters who decide elections are no longer a tidy group in the political centre. Many of them hold views that do not fit the usual left and right map: cautious on spending, sceptical of large institutions, worried about the cost of living and about the pace of change.

Parties that chase an imagined moderate voter can end up speaking to almost nobody. The people they are trying to reach do not see themselves as centrists at all. They see themselves as ordinary, and they feel overlooked.

None of this means the two-party system is finished. First past the post rewards size, and it punishes new parties harshly. What it does mean is that majorities will be harder to win and harder to keep. Expect more volatile results, more seats changing hands on small swings, and more surprises on election night.
The parties that adapt will be the ones that stop treating voters as a fixed map to be won, and start treating them as people who can, and will, walk away.
